title: Garter-stitch scarf
subtitle: The first finished object every knitter makes.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in garter stitch on 5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn. The reversible, non-curling fabric makes it the ideal first project for a new knitter, and the finished scarf measures 20 cm wide by 180 cm long.
sourceNotes: Garter stitch scarves appear throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s), where plain knitting on every row is recommended for beginners and for warm accessories. Cornelia Mee, A Manual of Knitting and Crochet (1846), Internet Archive, describes the same construction for comforter scarves.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cast-on method that forms a neat, elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn together over two fingers. Produces one row of knitting as it sets up.
The fabric produced when every row is knitted. Both faces show the same horizontal ridges, the fabric lies flat without curling, and it has the same appearance on the right and wrong sides.
The process of removing stitches from the needle to form a finished edge. The standard method knits two stitches then passes the first over the second, repeating to the end.
Wetting or steaming the finished knitted piece and pinning it to shape while it dries, to set the stitches and open the fabric to its full dimensions.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat from one end to the other in
garter stitch

, finishing at 20 cm wide and 180 cm long. Every row is a knit row, which means the fabric lies flat, shows the same ridged texture on both sides, and never curls at the edges. A knitter who can work a knit stitch can finish this scarf; no purling, no shaping, no seaming.

The scarf is worked flat from cast-on to cast-off, which is the simplest possible construction for a rectangular piece. Flat construction was chosen because garter stitch on straight needles needs nothing else: the cast-on forms the short edge, every row builds length, and the cast-off finishes the opposite short edge. The finished piece needs about 200 g (360 m / 393 yards) of aran-weight yarn, which makes a warm, substantial scarf that wraps comfortably twice around the neck.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any aran-weight yarn. Wool or wool-blend gives the most stretch and warmth; cotton gives a heavier, cooler scarf.

items.name: 5 mm straight or circular needles (UK 6 / US 8)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular, any length from 40 cm up
items.substitutions: Circular needles work just as well for flat knitting.

items.name: Blocking mat and rust-proof pins
items.substitutions: A folded towel and ordinary pins work if you don't have a blocking mat.

content.text: Gauge

18 sts x 36 rows = 10 x 10 cm in garter stitch on 5 mm needles, blocked. Work a 15 cm square swatch and measure across the centre once it has dried after blocking. Each stitch off gauge changes the finished width by about 1 cm: a gauge of 17 sts per 10 cm produces a scarf 21 cm wide rather than 20 cm; 19 sts per 10 cm gives 19 cm. Each two rows off gauge across the full 648-row scarf adds or removes about 5 cm of finished length.
Stitches used

K (knit): insert the right needle from left to right through the front of the stitch, wrap the yarn counterclockwise around the right needle tip, and draw the loop through to the right side. The whole scarf uses only this stitch.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 36 stitches on the needle. Before you begin, measure off a tail long enough for the cast-on using the formula: tail_cm = (needle circumference in mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For a 5 mm needle (circumference approximately 15.7 mm) and 36 stitches: (15.7 x 36) / 10 + 15 = 56.5 + 15 = about 72 cm. Leave a tail of at least 72 cm before making your slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on, count your stitches. You should have 36 stitches on the needle.
Body
Every row: K to end. (36 sts)

Work every row the same until the scarf measures 180 cm from the cast-on edge, measured along the straight grain with the piece lying flat. This takes approximately 648 rows in the stated gauge. At the halfway mark (about 90 cm), count the stitches again: you should still have 36 stitches.
Cast off
Using the standard
cast off

: K2, then pass the first stitch over the second. K1, pass the second stitch over. Continue to the last stitch, then cut the yarn leaving a 15 cm tail and pull it through the final loop. Work loosely: if the cast-off edge pulls in, cast off on a needle one size larger.
Common faults

Stitch count drifts up across the length. The most common cause is accidentally knitting into the loop below the first stitch on the needle when starting a new row, which adds a stitch. Always insert the needle tip cleanly through the first stitch only.
Tight cast-off that flips the top edge. This happens when the cast-off row is worked at the same tension as the body. Use a needle one size larger for the cast-off row, or deliberately work loosely.

Uneven edge stitches. The selvedge can look loopy or puckered if the first and last stitches of each row are worked at a different tension from the rest. Some knitters slip the first stitch of every row without working it; this tightens the edges and produces a neat chain edge. Try one or two rows with slipped selvedges to see if it suits your tension.

Scarf shorter or longer than planned. Gauge in garter stitch varies more across row count than stitch count. Always measure the body length along the straight grain, not along the edge, and measure while the piece is lying flat, not stretched.
Finishing

Thread the cast-on tail and the cast-off tail onto the darning needle and weave each through five or six stitches along the wrong-side edge, changing direction once to secure. Trim the ends close to the fabric.
Wet
blocking

is recommended for wool. Soak the scarf in cool water for 20 minutes, press out the water without wringing, roll in a towel to remove excess moisture, then pin to shape on a blocking mat and leave to dry flat overnight. Garter stitch relaxes and evens out after a good soak.
Care

For wool: handwash in cool water with a small amount of wool wash, support the wet weight of the scarf, and lay flat to dry. Do not wring. For cotton: machine wash gentle on a cool cycle and lay flat to dry. For acrylic: cool machine wash on a gentle cycle; do not tumble dry.
What to try next

The garter-stitch scarf is the foundation. From here, try the 1x1 ribbed scarf, which introduces purling and produces a stretchy, reversible fabric with more texture. Or cast on the same 36 stitches in a contrast yarn and work in stripes, changing colour every ten rows to use up yarn ends.
